addressed_problems.content: Despite the use of Jaccard similarity between binary masks to quantify sub-network overlap across languages in mBERT, this coarse measure does not capture the fine-grained parameter-level identity of language-neutral versus language-specific components; consequently, it remains unresolved which exact parameters—by layer, attention head, or neuron—encode shared cross-lingual information and which are language-specific, limiting the ability to predict small differences in cross-lingual transfer performance from sub-network overlap alone.

The analysis relies exclusively on iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) derived from the lottery ticket hypothesis to discover language-specific sub-networks; whether alternative pruning or mask-discovery approaches—such as structured pruning, learned masks, Fisher-information-based importance, or composable sparse fine-tuning—would identify the same set of language-neutral parameters, or would reveal a different division of neutral and language-specific components, remains an unverified open question.

The experiments cover only three tasks (masked language modeling, named entity recognition, and natural language inference); whether the observed existence of language-neutral sub-networks and their effective cross-lingual transferability generalizes to other NLP tasks—such as question answering, machine translation, or text generation—is an open empirical question, as those tasks may impose different representational demands that alter the balance between language-neutral and language-specific parameters.

The study evaluates eleven typologically diverse languages, but does not include extremely low-resource languages with limited pre-training data or languages from underrepresented families; whether the language-neutral sub-networks persist and transfer effectively for such languages, which may contribute less to the model's pre-trained parameters, remains an open empirical question that would test the universality of the findings.

The primary experiments use mBERT (110M parameters), with additional validation on mT5 (580M parameters) for a single task; whether the phenomenon of language-neutral sub-networks scales to larger multilingual models, such as XLM-R Large or models with billions of parameters, where capacity and representational partitioning may differ, is an unresolved empirical question.

The study establishes a correlation between sub-network overlap and cross-lingual transfer performance, but does not provide causal evidence that the identified language-neutral parameters are directly responsible for successful transfer; it remains open whether the observed transfer benefits stem from the neutral parameters themselves or from confounding factors such as dataset overlap, tokenizer characteristics, or shared vocabulary, necessitating causal intervention experiments (e.g., ablating neutral parameters) to disentangle these effects.

While cross-lingual transferability of sub-networks degrades at higher sparsity levels (e.g., 80% vs. 50%), the exact sparsity threshold at which language-neutral components are critically pruned, causing notable transfer loss, has not been determined; identifying this threshold would clarify the minimal sub-network size required to retain language-neutral capacity and guide efficient multilingual model deployment.

Multilingual pre-trained language models (MultiLMs) such as mBERT are widely used because a model fine-tuned on data from one language often generalizes to the same task in other languages. However, it is unsettled which aspects of these models enable cross-lingual transfer: prior studies disagree on whether MultiLMs learn a single, language-neutral internal representation or whether they partition capacity into language-specific subspaces. Most prior analyses probe contextual representations (outputs) for language-neutral structure, leaving open whether language-neutrality is present at the level of model parameters and which parameters encode language-neutral versus language-specific information. Existing probing approaches also depend on representational-similarity metrics whose invariances can alter conclusions. Practically, this uncertainty prevents principled methods to (a) identify parameter subsets that are reusable across languages, (b) predict when parameter reuse will yield strong zero-shot transfer, and (c) design pruning or modularization strategies that preserve cross-lingual generalization. Consequently, there is a need for (i) a parameter-level operationalization of language-neutrality that can be measured and manipulated, (ii) methods to extract per-language parameter sub-networks in pre-trained MultiLMs with fidelity to the original model's performance, and (iii) empirical quantification of how much sub-network overlap across languages explains cross-lingual transfer and how pruning density affects the retention of language-neutral components.

nodes.content: In cross-lingual transfer research, analyses have predominantly focused on contextual output representations and on heuristic similarity metrics, which does not directly reveal whether the same model parameters are reused across languages. Researchers needed a parameter-level operational definition and a reproducible protocol to: extract compact sub-networks that retain task performance, quantify overlap between those sub-networks, and evaluate whether a sub-network discovered for one language can serve as an effective initialization for another. Prior work lacked (a) a clear mask-based definition of language-neutrality, (b) a transfer test that isolates parameter reuse (re-initializing to original pretrained weights), and (c) an integrated methodology to discover and evaluate such masks across languages and tasks. Without these, it was impossible to attribute cross-lingual transfer to specific parameter overlap or to test how pruning density affects the preservation of language-neutral components.

To study parameter-level language neutrality one needs sub-networks that (i) can be reliably discovered from a pre-trained MultiLM, and (ii) achieve near-original performance in isolation so that subsequent transfer experiments probe language-neutral versus language-specific components rather than gross degradation from poor pruning. Prior pruning approaches and evaluations were not standardized for this multilingual transfer setting: without a clear iterative-pruning protocol tied to the original pretrained initialization and an explicit winning-ticket criterion tied to the original model's variance, it was unclear which pruning method yields sub-networks suitable for cross-lingual transfer experiments.

Before these experiments it was unclear whether pre-trained MultiLMs contain sparse, trainable sub-networks for each language-task pair that achieve near-original performance when trained in isolation. Determining existence is necessary because subsequent cross-lingual transfer analyses require sub-networks that are themselves high-quality solutions; if such sub-networks did not exist, transfer experiments would conflate the absence of transfer with the inability to find competitive sparse models. The paper resolves whether competitive per-language per-task sparse sub-networks can be found from a single pretrained mBERT initialization and provides the sparsity regimes where they do and do not exist.

To interpret cross-lingual transfer at the parameter level, one must know whether sub-networks for different languages share parameters, and whether this sharing is uniform across model depth and tasks. Prior work lacked a quantified, layerwise account of how much parameter reuse occurs across languages and tasks. Without such measurements there is no empirical basis to argue that shared parameters could plausibly underpin observed zero-shot behavior or to identify which layers preserve cross-lingual commonality versus language specialization.

Even if parameter overlap exists, it was unknown whether that overlap corresponds to parameters usable as initializations for other languages in a way that preserves performance. This is the critical test of whether parameter-level sharing is functionally language-neutral: unless a source-language sub-network can be transferred and re-trained to achieve near-native performance on another language-task pair, overlap alone is insufficient evidence of language-neutral representation. The paper resolves this by directly measuring $a(s,t)$ vs $a(t,t)$ across tasks and languages, demonstrating that for several tasks (notably XNLI and NER) parameter-level transfer is practically effective, whereas for MLM it is more limited.

Even if language-neutral parameters exist at moderate sparsity, it was unresolved how pruning density affects which components survive: do language-neutral parameters persist even in very sparse models, or are they among the parameters removed? Answering this is important for understanding trade-offs between compression (sparsity) and cross-lingual generalization. The experiments clarify that moderate sparsity (e.g., 50%) preserves cross-lingual components better than aggressive sparsity (e.g., 80%), revealing a structural separation of neutral versus specific parameters by resilience to pruning.

A concern was that the observed parameter-level language-neutrality might be an artifact of mBERT's architecture, training corpus, or tokenizer rather than a general property of MultiLMs. Demonstrating similar behavior on a distinct multilingual model (mT5) is necessary to generalize findings and to justify claims about MultiLMs more broadly. The cross-model experiments address this gap.

A stronger test of language-neutrality is whether sub-networks can serve as language-agnostic feature extractors in zero-shot settings unrelated to the discovery task. Prior analyses focused on representational similarity or task transfer; evaluating parallel-sentence retrieval with transferred sparse sub-networks probes whether the discovered parameters encode general-purpose multilingual semantics. Demonstrating that XNLI-derived sub-networks can match full-model retrieval accuracy provides evidence they capture robust semantic features transferable without language-specific fine-tuning.

The theoretical distinction between shared/interlingual parameters and language-specific parameters had been hypothesized but not demonstrated at parameter granularity in pretrained MultiLMs. Researchers needed empirical evidence that such a decomposition exists, that it is detectable via pruning and transfer tests, and that it has operational consequences (i.e., pruning density shifts the balance between neutral and specific components). Resolving this clarifies mechanistic explanations for zero-shot transfer and indicates where pruning or modularization can preserve cross-lingual behavior.

If language-neutral parameters are desirable, it is important to know whether discovery procedures can be adjusted to favor neutral components (e.g., by using multilingual data during pruning) rather than producing sub-networks biased toward a single language. Prior per-language pruning left this question open. The combined-language pruning experiment addresses whether mixing languages at discovery time yields sub-networks with broader cross-lingual utility.

Language-neutrality of a multilingual model is operationalized as the overlap between language-encoding sub-networks: a multilingual language model (MultiLM) is considered more language-neutral to the extent that the binary masks $m\in\{0,1\}^{|\theta|}$ that define high-performing sub-networks $f(x; m \odot \theta)$ for different languages share parameters. An evaluation protocol follows: (1) discover language-task-specific sub-networks by iterative unstructured magnitude pruning (training the model to peak performance on the task, pruning the 10% lowest-magnitude parameters from the original pre-trained initialization $\theta_0$, resetting the remaining parameters to $\theta_0$, and repeating for $n = s/10$ rounds to reach target sparsity $s$), producing masks $m$ and corresponding sparse sub-networks $f(x;m\odot\theta_0)$; (2) assess language-neutrality by transferring a discovered mask $m_s$ for source language $s$ to a target language $t$ by re-initializing the remaining (unpruned) parameters to their original pre-trained values $\theta_0$ and re-training on the target language task; (3) compare transferred performance $a(s,t)$ to the target-language native sub-network performance $a(t,t)$ and measure parameter-level overlap via the Jaccard index $\frac{|m_s\cap m_t|}{|m_s\cup m_t|}$. This framing explicitly defines sub-network, winning ticket, mask overlap, and the transfer test used to quantify parameter-level language-neutrality.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 1 is a definitional framing and evaluation protocol, not an empirical claim. No load-bearing weak points were identified because the operationalization is given as a premise of the analysis, not derived from evidence. No highlights were identified because the protocol is clearly specified but does not involve a strength beyond standard methodological practice. The conclusion's usefulness depends on its acceptance as a valid operationalization; the empirical validation comes from subsequent conclusions.

nodes.title: Parameter-level framing of language-neutrality and evaluation protocol

nodes.content: Iterative unstructured magnitude pruning (the lottery ticket protocol) is applied to a pre-trained multilingual language model (MultiLM) by: (a) training the model to peak performance on a task, (b) pruning the $p\%$ lowest-magnitude parameters from the original initialization $\theta_0$ (with $p=10$), (c) resetting remaining parameters to $\theta_0$, and (d) repeating for $n=\frac{s}{p}$ rounds to reach target sparsity $s$. A sub-network $f(x;m\odot\theta_0)$ is treated as a winning ticket if its maximum evaluation performance $a'$ satisfies $a - a' \leq \epsilon$ where $a$ is the original pre-trained MultiLM's peak performance on the task and $\epsilon$ is set to one standard deviation of the original MultiLM's performance on the task. This procedure produces masks $m$ and corresponding sparse sub-networks $f(x;m\odot\theta_0)$ that are subsequently used for cross-lingual transfer experiments.

metadata.narrative: The pruning method and winning-ticket definition (Conclusion 2) are clearly specified and follow established lottery-ticket literature. The single load-bearing weak point (P1) concerns the statistical instability of the epsilon threshold due to estimation from only three runs; if the true variance were substantially different, the set of sub-networks classified as winning tickets could shift, affecting all subsequent experiments. However, the threshold choice is a standard convention, and many sub-networks comfortably exceed it (Figure 2), so the practical impact is likely limited to marginal cases. No highlight offsets this risk directly, but the method's transparency and reproducibility (H1 provides indirect support for the discovery method's reliability) are positive. The conclusion overall is credible, with a modest caveat about threshold sensitivity.

nodes.title: Concrete pruning method and winning-ticket definition for multilingual language models (MultiLMs)

nodes.content: For the multilingual BERT (mBERT) model, winning tickets (sub-networks $f^{*}(x;m\odot\theta_0)$ that achieve a maximum evaluation performance $a'$ satisfying $a - a' \leq \epsilon$, where $a$ is the full mBERT model's peak performance on the task and $\epsilon$ is one standard deviation of the full mBERT model's performance) are discovered for each examined language and task (masked language modeling (MLM), named entity recognition (NER), and cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI)) at multiple sparsity levels; many language-task pairs admit winning tickets at 50% sparsity and in several cases at other sparsity thresholds specified per language/task. As sub-networks become sparser beyond those thresholds, they often cease to meet the winning-ticket criterion, though they frequently retain performance within roughly 10% of their best sparse performance. This establishes that task- and language-specific sparse sub-networks that match the full mBERT model's performance (within the chosen variance criterion of one standard deviation) exist in mBERT.

metadata.narrative: The existence of winning tickets per language-task pair (Conclusion 3) is convincingly demonstrated across 11 languages and 3 tasks at multiple sparsity levels. The highlight (H1) shows that the discovered sub-networks are highly reproducible across random seeds (98.66% mask overlap for NER), establishing that they are not artifacts of individual runs. No load-bearing weak points were identified: the existence claim is directly supported by the empirical data (Figure 2, Table 2). The only qualification — that not all sparsity levels yield winning tickets — is part of the conclusion itself. The high reproducibility underwrites the reliability of the sub-network discovery for all subsequent experiments that depend on these sub-networks.

nodes.title: Existence of winning tickets per language and task in multilingual BERT (mBERT)

nodes.content: For the multilingual BERT (mBERT) model, masks $m$ discovered for different languages exhibit non-trivial absolute parameter overlap: at 50% sparsity the empirically observed Jaccard similarities between language sub-networks are substantially above the random expectation (33% for independent 50% masks). The per-task ordering of overlap is: named entity recognition (NER) shows the largest pairwise overlap across languages, followed by cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI), then masked language modeling (MLM). Layerwise patterns differ by task: for NER and XNLI the overlap generally increases in higher layers, while for MLM overlap increases up to middle layers and then decreases in upper layers. Same-language masks discovered with different random seeds yield much higher overlaps (e.g., average intra-language overlap across runs is 98.66 for NER, 92.23 for XNLI, and 92.23 for MLM), indicating that cross-language overlaps are meaningfully lower than identical-language variability.

metadata.narrative: The parameter-overlap patterns (Conclusion 4) are direct empirical observations from Figure 3. No load-bearing uncertain bridges were identified: the Jaccard similarities are measured at a single sparsity level (50%), but the conclusion explicitly confines itself to that regime. The cross-language overlaps are clearly above the random expectation of 33%, and the layerwise patterns are reported descriptively. No highlight rises above standard reporting; the overlap patterns themselves are the conclusion's content. The descriptive nature of this conclusion makes it robust, though the generalizability to other sparsity levels is an open question (not claimed by the paper).

nodes.title: Parameter-overlap patterns across languages and layers in mBERT

nodes.content: For the mBERT model, when a mask $m_s$ discovered for source language $s$ is transferred to target language $t$ by re-initializing the remaining (unpruned) parameters to their original pre-trained values $\theta_0$ and re-training on $t$, the transferred sub-network $f(x;m_s\odot\theta_0)$ often reaches performance close to the native target sub-network $f(x;m_t\odot\theta_0)$. For named entity recognition (NER), most target languages retain roughly 98% of the target sub-network's performance when trained from a source-language mask rather than from a random mask (where each parameter is independently kept with probability 0.5). For cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI), many source-language masks transfer so well that English and French masks are winning tickets for other languages (i.e., $a(s,t)$ is within one standard deviation of $a(t,t)$). In some cases transferred sub-networks outperform the full mBERT model on low-resource target languages (e.g., the Arabic winning ticket improves performance by approximately 1.5 percentage points on Swahili and Urdu). In contrast, masked language modeling (MLM) masks show limited transfer (larger perplexity drops), but still outperform random 50% masks by a substantial margin.

metadata.narrative: The claim that transferred sub-networks often enable effective cross-lingual transfer (Conclusion 5) is supported by strong positive evidence (H2) for XNLI: English and French masks are winning tickets for all other languages, and Arabic masks outperform the full model on low-resource languages. These results are uncontaminated by the weak point (P2) because English and French have winning tickets at 50% sparsity. However, P2 identifies a methodological confound for Urdu (XNLI) and Farsi/Urdu (NER), where sub-optimal sparsity is used, potentially making their transfer performance appear worse than it would be with true winning-ticket masks. This narrows the conclusion's scope: the main finding holds firmly for high-resource languages with winning tickets at 50% sparsity, but the claim that low-resource languages have more language-specific sub-networks is less robust due to this confound. The overall pattern — that many transferred sub-networks enable effective transfer — stands, with a caveat for a few language-task pairs.

nodes.title: Transferred sub-networks often enable effective cross-lingual transfer within the same task

nodes.content: For the mBERT model on the NER and XNLI tasks, increasing sparsity of discovered sub-networks degrades cross-lingual transferability: sub-networks at 80% sparsity show substantially larger average relative performance drops (defined as $\frac{1}{|L|-1} \sum_{t \in L \setminus s} \frac{a(s,t)-a(t,t)}{a(t,t)}$ where $s$ is the source language and $L$ is the set of languages for the task) when transferred across languages than sub-networks at 50% sparsity. This indicates that parameters facilitating cross-lingual transfer (the language-neutral components) are preferentially removed as pruning becomes more aggressive, leaving language- and task-specific parameters to dominate the remaining capacity.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that sparsity reduces transferability by preferentially removing language-neutral components (Conclusion 6) is critically weakened by a confounding factor (P3): the 80% sparse sub-networks are not winning tickets, so the comparison conflates sparsity with sub-network quality. The descriptive fact that higher sparsity degrades transfer remains true, but the mechanistic interpretation that language-neutral components are selectively pruned is not supported by the evidence as presented. No highlight addresses this confound. The conclusion's value is thus limited to the empirical observation, while the causal claim about language-neutral components is unsubstantiated within this experiment.

nodes.title: Sparsity reduces transferability: language-neutral components are pruned at high sparsity

nodes.content: The pattern that many language-discovered sub-networks transfer well within the same task is observed beyond the multilingual BERT (mBERT) model: experiments on the multilingual text-to-text transformer (mT5) for cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI) at 50% sparsity show relatively small transfer performance drops, and similar-language masks (English, Spanish, French, German) transfer well to other languages, indicating that parameter-level language-neutral components are present in multiple multilingual language model (MultiLM) architectures.

metadata.narrative: The generalization to mT5 (Conclusion 7) is substantively weakened by P4: the mT5 sub-networks used at 50% sparsity are not winning tickets, whereas the mBERT experiments rely on winning tickets. The similarity of transfer patterns could reflect properties of any 50% sparse mask rather than language-neutral components specific to high-quality sub-networks. The mT5 result is consistent with the mBERT findings but does not provide equivalent evidence. No highlight compensates for this quality gap. Thus, while the conclusion is plausible, it is not robustly supported by the experiments as designed.

nodes.title: Phenomenon generalizes across multilingual architectures (mT5)

nodes.content: Sub-networks discovered via cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI) pruning on the multilingual BERT (mBERT) model produce contextual features that are effective for zero-shot parallel sentence retrieval (on the WMT14 English-to-French dataset, 3003 sentence pairs): XNLI-winning tickets (sub-networks that achieve performance within one standard deviation of the full mBERT model on the XNLI task) reach higher parallel-retrieval accuracy than masked language modeling (MLM)- or named entity recognition (NER)-derived sub-networks and, for some layers (the middle layers), match the full mBERT model's retrieval accuracy. Across tasks, middle layers yield increased similarity and retrieval performance, consistent with these layers encoding cross-lingual semantic information useful for sentence-level semantics.

metadata.narrative: The zero-shot retrieval result (Conclusion 8) benefits from a positive finding (H3): XNLI-winning tickets approach full-model accuracy on English-to-French retrieval, and middle layers are most effective. This provides independent evidence that the sub-networks capture cross-lingual semantic features useful outside their discovery task. However, P5 limits the strength of the conclusion: the absence of a random sub-network baseline means that the retrieval success could be due to any structured 50% mask rather than language-neutral components specifically, and the single language pair (English-French) restricts generalizability. H3 preempts the alternative that sub-networks are not useful for feature extraction, while P5 constrains the scope to the tested pair. The conclusion is moderately supported, with the need for a random baseline and more language pairs remaining as uncertainties.

nodes.title: Task-conditioned sub-networks capture transferable semantic features used in zero-shot retrieval

nodes.content: Empirically, multilingual language models (MultiLMs) (as exemplified by the multilingual BERT (mBERT) and multilingual text-to-text transformer (mT5) models) contain two separable parameter components: (a) language-neutral parameters that are shared across languages, survive moderate pruning (e.g., 50% sparsity), and facilitate cross-lingual transfer and zero-shot semantic tasks (e.g., parallel sentence retrieval); and (b) language- and task-specific parameters that are more sensitive to pruning and are required to fully recover native target-language performance, especially at high sparsity. Thus, cross-lingual transfer is enabled by a combination of shared parameter subsets and a complementary set of language-specific parameters.

metadata.narrative: The central theoretical claim that multilingual models decompose into language-neutral and language-specific parameter components (Conclusion 9) is the most ambitious conclusion. It benefits from substantial converging evidence (H4) across five independent experimental approaches, which makes the interpretation much more than a single-experiment narrative. However, P6 highlights that all evidence is correlational: no causal intervention directly tests whether the shared parameters perform the same function across languages. The anomalous NER case (high overlap but poor transfer) further suggests that the decomposition may not be uniform across tasks. The convergence (H4) provides substantive credibility, but the lack of causal validation (P6) means the decomposition remains a well-supported hypothesis rather than a demonstrated fact. The paper's claim is appropriately cautious, but the conclusion's strength is moderate due to the gap between correlation and causation.

nodes.title: Multilingual models decompose into language-neutral and language-specific parameter components

nodes.content: Pruning the multilingual BERT (mBERT) model on a combined multi-language training corpus (English, Farsi, French, and Chinese, each contributing 5000 samples for a balanced total of 20,000 training examples) yields a single 50%-sparse sub-network that, when transferred to several other languages for the named entity recognition (NER) task, outperforms sub-networks discovered from individual languages for three out of five evaluated target languages (Arabic, Russian, Urdu). This demonstrates that jointly pruning on multiple languages can increase the language-neutrality of the discovered sub-network.

metadata.narrative: The claim that combining multiple languages for pruning recovers more language-neutral sub-networks (Conclusion 10) is based on a single NER experiment with one language combination, where the improvement is observed for 3 of 5 target languages (P7). The result is interesting and suggestive but not broadly supported. No highlight offsets this narrow empirical base. The conclusion is preliminary: it warrants further investigation across tasks and language combinations, but in its current form it does not constitute a robust general result.

nodes.title: Combining multiple languages for pruning can recover more language-neutral sub-networks

nodes.content: The winning ticket criterion sets $\epsilon$ to one standard deviation of the original multilingual BERT (mBERT) model's performance, but that standard deviation is estimated from only three independent fine-tuning runs (all results are averages of three runs). With only three observations, the sample standard deviation has wide confidence intervals, and a different number of runs or different seeds could yield a substantially different threshold, potentially changing which sub-networks are classified as winning tickets for a given language-task pair.

metadata.failure_mode: If the estimated standard deviation is too small (by chance), the epsilon threshold is too tight, and some sub-networks that are functionally good and reproducible may be excluded, reducing the pool of winning tickets for later experiments. If the estimate is too large, the threshold is too lax, and poor sub-networks could be admitted, weakening the conclusions about transfer and language-neutrality that depend on high-quality sub-networks. Concretely, the existence of winning tickets for certain languages (conclusion 3) could change, and the transfer experiments (conclusion 5) would be affected if the sub-networks used are not all of guaranteed quality.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not report the individual standard deviations or justify the threshold choice against the small sample size. In the LTH literature, the winning ticket criterion is often defined with respect to the original model's accuracy directly (within a fixed margin), but here the margin is data-dependent and based on a noisy estimate. With n=3, the 95% confidence interval for the population standard deviation spans roughly 0.4 to 5 times the sample standard deviation, meaning the epsilon threshold could be off by a factor of several, and a different threshold would change which sub-networks meet the criterion.

nodes.title: Unstable winning-ticket threshold due to small sample for variance estimate

nodes.content:
In the cross-lingual transfer experiments for cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI) at a fixed 50% sparsity on mBERT, the Urdu winning ticket (a sub-network that meets the winning ticket criterion) exists only at 30% sparsity, yet a 50% sparse Urdu sub-network is used, which has native accuracy 63.13% compared to the full mBERT model's 63.06%, not within one standard deviation (i.e., not a winning ticket). For the named entity recognition (NER) task, Farsi and Urdu have winning tickets at 60% sparsity, but 50% sub-networks are used for all languages in the transfer experiments.
      Fig. 4c
      Table 2

metadata.failure_mode: If the non-winning-ticket 50% Urdu XNLI sub-network's poor quality (rather than language-specificity) causes its relatively poor transfer performance (both as source and target in Figure 4c), then the conclusion that Urdu sub-networks are language-specific is not supported. Similarly, if 60% winning tickets for Farsi and Urdu NER were used instead of 50% sub-networks, the NER transfer patterns might change, potentially altering the comparative picture across languages. The scope of damage is a narrowing of the conclusion: the claim that transferred sub-networks enable effective cross-lingual transfer holds for high-resource languages with winning tickets at 50% sparsity, but is not robustly demonstrated for languages that require different sparsity levels.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper acknowledges these discrepancies but still uses the sub-optimal sparsity for consistency. For Urdu XNLI, the 50% sub-network's native performance is essentially at the full model level (63.13 vs 63.06), but it is not classified as a winning ticket because the threshold is tighter; however, the performance is still low compared to other languages' native sub-network performance (e.g., English 82.14). For Farsi and Urdu NER, the 50% sub-networks are further from the winning ticket quality. The confound between sub-network quality and language-specificity makes the transfer results for these languages unreliable indicators of inherent language-neutrality.

nodes.title: Use of non‑winning‑ticket sparsity for Urdu (XNLI) and Farsi/Urdu (NER) in transfer

nodes.content:
In the comparison of cross-lingual transfer performance between sub-networks at 50% and 80% sparsity for the multilingual BERT (mBERT) model on named entity recognition (NER) and cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI) tasks, the 80% sparse sub-networks do not meet the winning ticket criterion (their performance is far below one standard deviation of the full mBERT model's performance on the same task), while most 50% sparse sub-networks do. The transfer degradation at 80% sparsity is therefore observed on sub-networks that are not high-quality models, confounding sparsity level with sub-network quality.
      Fig. 2
      Fig. 6

metadata.failure_mode: If the confound is not controlled, the claim that language-neutral components are preferentially pruned at high sparsity loses its primary experimental support. The observation that higher sparsity hurts transfer remains descriptively true, but the mechanism (selective pruning of neutral components) is not established. The conclusion would be reduced to a correlation between sparsity and transfer, not a demonstration of structural separation. This weakens the paper's main decomposition argument (conclusion 9) which relies on this result.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper attributes the transfer drop to the loss of language-neutral components, but the experiment does not control for overall model quality. At 80% sparsity, the sub-networks are simply worse at the task in general (as seen by low native performance), so their poor transfer could stem from general performance degradation rather than specific removal of language-neutral parameters. Without a matched-quality control (e.g., using sub-networks at both sparsities that achieve comparable native performance, or isolating the effect of sparsity on transfer while holding native quality constant), the causal interpretation is confounded.

nodes.title: Confounding of sparsity with sub‑network quality in 50% vs 80% comparison

nodes.content:
For the cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI) task on the multilingual text-to-text transformer (mT5) at 50% sparsity, the sub-networks used in cross-lingual transfer experiments are not winning tickets: winning tickets for these languages are not found at this sparsity level, and the absolute performance of these sub-networks (e.g., English accuracy 80.64% vs full mT5 83.13%) shows a drop larger than one standard deviation would allow.
      Fig. 5

metadata.failure_mode: If the mT5 sub-networks are not winning tickets, the similarity of transfer patterns between mBERT and mT5 may be coincidental or due to different underlying mechanisms. The conclusion that language-neutral components are present in multiple MultiLM architectures would be supported only by weaker evidence, and the claim about mT5 specifically would be limited to "some sparse sub-networks show transfer" rather than "winning-ticket-level language-neutral components exist." This narrows the generalizability of the core finding.
metadata.weakness_reason: The mT5 experiments are intended to show that the language-neutral parameter phenomenon generalizes beyond mBERT. However, the sub-networks used are not high-quality winning tickets, unlike the mBERT experiments where winning tickets are central. The observed transfer patterns on mT5 could reflect properties of any 50% sparse mask (e.g., retention of generally important parameters) rather than language-neutral components specific to winning tickets. The absence of winning tickets in mT5 undermines the claim that the same type of language-neutral sub-networks exist in other architectures.

nodes.title: mT5 sub‑networks are not winning tickets

nodes.content:
In the parallel sentence retrieval evaluation on the WMT14 English-to-French dataset (3003 sentence pairs), sub-networks from cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI), named entity recognition (NER), and masked language modeling (MLM) at 50% sparsity from the multilingual BERT (mBERT) model are used as feature extractors. The retrieval accuracy is compared only across these three sub-networks and the full mBERT model; no random 50% sparse sub-network baseline is included.
      Fig. 7

metadata.failure_mode: If a random 50% sparse sub-network achieved comparable retrieval accuracy, the conclusion that XNLI sub-networks capture transferable semantic features would be unsupported; the retrieval performance could be attributed to any structured preservation of embedding space, not specifically to language-neutral components from XNLI. This would weaken the evidence for conclusion 9 that these sub-networks encode general-purpose multilingual semantics.
metadata.weakness_reason: Without a random 50% sparse mask baseline, it is unclear whether the retrieval performance of XNLI-winning tickets is due to language-neutral semantic features or simply to the fact that any structured 50% mask (including randomly pruned ones that preserve general multilingual capacity) can achieve similar results. The paper shows XNLI tickets perform better than NER and MLM tickets, but the comparison does not isolate language-neutrality from task-specific feature preservation. Additionally, testing only English-to-French limits confidence in cross-lingual semantic feature extraction more broadly.

nodes.title: Missing random baseline and single language pair in retrieval

nodes.content:
The claim that multilingual BERT (mBERT) contains two separable parameter components — language-neutral and language-specific — is drawn from correlational patterns: (a) sub-network mask overlap across languages is above random, (b) cross-lingual transfer of winning tickets achieves near-native performance for cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI) and strong performance for named entity recognition (NER), (c) increasing sparsity reduces transfer, (d) similar patterns appear on the multilingual text-to-text transformer (mT5), and (e) multi-language pruning improves transfer. No experiment directly intervenes on the shared parameters (e.g., ablating them and measuring cross-lingual transfer) or verifies that shared parameters encode the same linguistic phenomena across languages via controlled perturbation.
      Fig. 3
      Fig. 4
      Fig. 6
      Fig. 5
      Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the decomposition is not causally real, the paper's central theoretical claim is an over-interpretation. The practical implications for parameter reuse, pruning strategies, and modularization would not follow from the evidence. The conclusion would be reduced to "sub-networks for different languages overlap and transfer well, and sparsity matters," which is still a useful empirical finding but not a structural decomposition of the model's parameters into functionally distinct types.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper uses the term "language-neutral components" as if it refers to a physically distinct set of parameters, but the evidence is entirely correlational: overlap correlates with transfer, sparsity hurts transfer, multi-language pruning helps. These patterns are consistent with the decomposition interpretation but also with alternative explanations (e.g., overall network capacity, task-specific feature reuse, tokenizer artifacts). Without a causal manipulation (e.g., removing the shared parameters and observing specific functional loss), the inference remains a plausible post-hoc interpretation rather than a demonstrated property of the model.

nodes.title: Correlational evidence only for decomposition

nodes.content:
In the multi-language pruning experiment on the multilingual BERT (mBERT) model, a single sub-network is discovered at 50% sparsity by combining 20,000 balanced named entity recognition (NER) training samples from English, Farsi, French, and Chinese (5000 per language). Its cross-lingual transfer performance on Arabic, German, Spanish, Russian, and Urdu is compared to sub-networks discovered from each language individually. The combined sub-network outperforms all individual sub-networks for 3 of the 5 target languages (Arabic, Russian, Urdu). No other task (masked language modeling (MLM), cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI)) or language combination is tested.
      Table 1

metadata.failure_mode: If the effect does not replicate on other tasks or language combinations, the conclusion that multi-language pruning recovers more language-neutral sub-networks would be limited to NER with the tested set of languages. The practical recommendation to use multilingual data during pruning would not be broadly supported. This narrows the claim from a general method to a task-specific observation.
metadata.weakness_reason: The experiment is restricted to a single task (NER) and a single combination of four languages. The improvement is observed for 3 of 5 target languages, which is a modest signal. Without replication on other tasks (e.g., XNLI, MLM) and with different language combinations, it is unclear whether multi-language pruning is a general method for increasing language-neutrality or a task- and combination-specific artifact. The balanced design with only 5k samples per language may also underrepresent each language, affecting the quality of the discovered sub-network.

nodes.title: Single‑task, single‑combination test for multi‑language pruning

nodes.content: When the iterative magnitude pruning procedure (training to peak performance, pruning the lowest-magnitude 10% of parameters from the original initialization, resetting remaining parameters to original values, repeated for five rounds) is applied with three different random seeds for the same language-task pair (English NER at 50% sparsity, XNLI at 50% sparsity, MLM at 50% sparsity), the resulting binary masks have average Jaccard similarities of 98.66 (NER), 92.23 (XNLI), and 92.23 (MLM) across the three runs.

metadata.credit: This high reproducibility demonstrates that the discovered sub-networks are not artifacts of a single fine-tuning trajectory or seed. Without this control, the per-language sub-networks could be idiosyncratic, and the subsequent cross-language overlap comparisons (conclusion 4) and transfer experiments (conclusion 5) would be uninterpretable — any observed overlap or transfer could be coincidental. The result underwrites the reliability of the sub-network discovery method for all conclusions that depend on these sub-networks (especially conclusions 3, 4, 5, 6, 9). The scope is full underwriting of the existence claim: winning tickets are stable features of the model, not run-specific noise.

nodes.title: High reproducibility of per‑language sub‑networks across seeds

nodes.content: For the XNLI task at 50% sparsity on mBERT, the winning ticket discovered for English, when transferred to any of nine other languages (Arabic, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Russian, Swahili, Urdu, Chinese), achieves accuracy within one standard deviation of each target language's native winning ticket accuracy. The French winning ticket is also a winning ticket for all other languages. The Arabic winning ticket, when transferred to Swahili and Urdu, achieves accuracy approximately 1.5 percentage points higher than the full mBERT model's native performance on those languages (70.29% vs 66.28% for Swahili, 70.29% vs 63.06% for Urdu).

metadata.credit: This finding provides direct empirical evidence that XNLI sub-networks for high-resource languages are functionally language-neutral at the parameter level: a mask discovered for one language can serve as an effective initialization for many others, even outperforming the full model for low-resource languages. The fact that English and French masks are winning tickets for every other language is a strong measure of parameter-level language-neutrality that goes beyond aggregate trends. Without this result, the claim that transferred sub-networks enable effective transfer would rest on average performance differences; this specific result shows that the transfer can be so complete that the transferred sub-network is indistinguishable from the native one (within the variance criterion). The credit scope is full underwriting of the claim that transferred sub-networks enable effective transfer within XNLI, and partial support for conclusion 9 (decomposition) by showing that shared parameters are sufficient for competitive performance.

nodes.title: English and French XNLI masks are winning tickets for all languages

nodes.content: For English-to-French parallel sentence retrieval on the WMT14 dataset (3003 sentence pairs), the 50% sparse XNLI-winning tickets used as feature extractors achieve top-5 retrieval accuracy close to that of the full mBERT model, with the best layer reaching within 1-2 percentage points of full model accuracy. The XNLI-winning tickets outperform both NER- and MLM-derived sub-networks, and retrieval accuracy correlates with layerwise cross-lingual mask overlap, peaking in middle layers (layers 6-9).

metadata.credit: This experiment demonstrates that sub-networks discovered for NLI not only transfer for the same task across languages (conclusion 5) but also serve as language-agnostic feature extractors for a different task (sentence retrieval) in a zero-shot setting — i.e., without any fine-tuning on retrieval. The correlation with layerwise overlap patterns strengthens the interpretation that shared parameters in middle layers encode multilingual semantic information. Without this result, the claim that winning tickets capture general-purpose multilingual semantics would rely solely on within-task transfer. The scope is partial underwriting of conclusion 8 (the sub-networks capture transferable semantic features) and additional independent support for conclusion 9 (decomposition), because it shows that task-neutral semantic features are preserved in the sub-networks.

nodes.title: XNLI sub‑networks match full model retrieval accuracy

nodes.content: Five distinct lines of evidence converge on the claim that multilingual models (specifically mBERT and mT5) contain separable language-neutral and language-specific parameter components: (1) sub-network mask overlap across languages is substantially above random expectation, (2) cross-lingual transfer of winning tickets achieves near-native performance for XNLI and strong performance for NER, (3) increasing sparsity from 50% to 80% degrades cross-lingual transfer, (4) similar transfer patterns are observed on mT5, and (5) pruning on a combined multilingual corpus yields sub-networks with broader cross-lingual utility.

metadata.credit: The convergence of multiple independent experiments, each with different methodological assumptions and potential confounds, provides stronger evidence for a latent parameter decomposition than any single experiment could. The core mBERT results (overlap, transfer, sparsity effects) establish the basic pattern; the mT5 result shows cross-model generality; the multi-language pruning result shows that discovery procedures can be manipulated to enhance language-neutrality. Together, these make the decomposition interpretation more than a post-hoc narrative by providing converging operationalizations. Without this convergence, the claim that language-neutral components exist would rely almost entirely on the XNLI transfer results (H2), which could be explained by task-specific properties. The scope is full underwriting of the claim that the decomposition is an empirically supported interpretation across multiple models and tasks, albeit not yet causally verified (as noted in P6).

nodes.title: Converging evidence from five independent experiments

steps.reasoning: Define a sub-network of a neural network: for any network $f(x; \theta)$ with initial parameters $\theta$, a sub-network is $f(x; m \odot \theta)$ where $m \in \{0,1\}^{|\theta|}$ is a binary mask on the parameters, and $\odot$ denotes element-wise product; the mask $m$ sets many parameters of the original network to zero and thus prunes edges in the computation graph.

Operationalize language-neutrality at the parameter level: language-neutrality is the degree to which the parameters learned for different languages are shared, measured as the overlap between the binary masks $m$ that define high-performing sub-networks $f(x; m \odot \theta)$ for different languages; explicitly, two sub-networks are more language-neutral with respect to each other the more their masks share parameters.

Specify the measure of parameter overlap used: given two binary masks $m_s$ and $m_t$ for source language $s$ and target language $t$, measure their parameter-level overlap by the Jaccard index $\frac{|m_s \cap m_t|}{|m_s \cup m_t|}$, where $|\cdot|$ denotes cardinality of the set of kept (1) parameters in the mask.

Describe the protocol to discover language-task-specific sub-networks: use iterative unstructured magnitude pruning (an iterative magnitude pruning procedure derived from the lottery ticket hypothesis) applied to a pre-trained initialization $\theta_0$ to produce masks $m$ and corresponding sparse sub-networks $f(x; m \odot \theta_0)$ that are tuned for a single language and task; this is the discovery step.
Frankle and Carbin (2019)

Describe the transfer evaluation test to quantify parameter-level language-neutrality: for a discovered mask $m_s$ from source language $s$, transfer it to a target language $t$ by (a) re-initializing the remaining (unpruned) parameters to their original pre-trained values $\theta_0$ (so the transferred sub-network is $f(x; m_s \odot \theta_0)$), and (b) re-training this sub-network on the target language task; measure the transferred performance as $a(s,t)$ and compare it to the native target-language sub-network performance $a(t,t)$ to assess how language-neutral the source mask is.

Summarize the evaluation steps as an explicit three-part protocol: (1) discover language-task-specific sub-networks by iterative magnitude pruning applied to pre-trained initialization $\theta_0$, producing masks $m$ and sub-networks $f(x; m \odot \theta_0)$; (2) assess language-neutrality by transferring a discovered mask $m_s$ to a target language $t$ via re-initialization to $\theta_0$ and re-training on $t$ to obtain $a(s,t)$; (3) quantify parameter-level overlap with the Jaccard index $\frac{|m_s \cap m_t|}{|m_s \cup m_t|}$ and compare $a(s,t)$ to $a(t,t)$ to evaluate transfer performance.
Fig. 1

Clarify terminology used in this framing: "sub-network" is $f(x; m \odot \theta)$ as defined; "winning ticket" will later be used to denote a sub-network that matches the full model's performance within a chosen tolerance; "mask overlap" is the Jaccard index above; and the "transfer test" is the re-initialize-and-retrain procedure described in the previous step.

Starting from the parameter-level framing and the definition of sub-networks $f(x; m \odot \theta)$ and pre-trained initialization $\theta_0$ (treat these as given), implement iterative unstructured magnitude pruning as the concrete pruning method to obtain language- and task-specific masks.

Specify the iterative pruning schedule and parameters: set the iterative pruning rate $p = 10\%$ (i.e., prune $p\%$ of parameters per round), and for a desired target sparsity $s$ compute the number of rounds $n = \frac{s}{p}$; in practice, $p=10$ is used so, for example, reaching $s=50\%$ sparsity requires five rounds.
Algorithm 1

Describe the round procedure precisely: in each pruning round $r$ (for $r = 0$ to $n-1$), train the network on the task to peak performance arriving at parameters $\theta_i$, prune the $p\%$ lowest-magnitude parameters with respect to the original initialization $\theta_0$ (i.e., remove the $p\%$ parameters of $\theta_0$ with smallest absolute magnitude), then reset the remaining parameters to their original pre-trained values in $\theta_0$, and proceed to the next round.
Han et al. (2015)

Define the winning-ticket criterion used to decide whether a discovered sub-network is a "winning ticket": denote by $a$ the original model's maximum evaluation performance when training the full network and by $a'$ the maximum evaluation performance attained by the sub-network $f(x; m \odot \theta_0)$ when trained in isolation; the sub-network is treated as a winning ticket if $a - a' \leq \epsilon$ and the sub-network reaches its peak performance no later than the full model (i.e., $i' \leq i$); set $\epsilon$ to one standard deviation of the original model's performance.

Record that this implementation yields explicit binary masks $m$ and corresponding sparse sub-networks $f(x; m \odot \theta_0)$ to be used in subsequent cross-lingual transfer experiments and overlap analyses; these masks and sub-networks are the operational artifacts of the method.

Starting from the pruning method and winning-ticket definition established earlier (treat those results as given), run the iterative magnitude pruning algorithm (with $p=10\%$ rounds to reach various sparsities) for each examined language and task on mBERT to discover candidate sub-networks $f^{*}(x; m \odot \theta_0)$.

Collect and evaluate the pruned sub-networks across sparsity levels from 0% to 90% for the three tasks (masked language modeling (MLM), named entity recognition (NER), and cross-lingual natural language inference (XNLI)), measuring task-specific evaluation metrics (perplexity for MLM, F1 for NER, accuracy for XNLI) on development sets averaged over three random seeds.
Fig. 2

Establish existence of winning tickets per language and task by applying the winning-ticket criterion ($a - a' \leq \epsilon$ with $\epsilon$ = one standard deviation): for each examined language and for each task, find sub-networks at multiple sparsity levels that satisfy the criterion and thus qualify as winning tickets; report that many language-task pairs admit winning tickets at 50% sparsity.
Fig. 2

Document the behavior as sparsity increases: note that as sub-networks become sparser beyond those threshold sparsities where winning tickets are found, they frequently cease to meet the winning-ticket criterion, although they often retain performance within roughly 10% of their best sparse performance; this trend is observed across tasks and languages in the plotted results.
Fig. 2

Support the claim with tabulated per-language results: consult the reported table of winning-ticket performances at their highest sparsity (showing e.g., perplexity, F1, accuracy per language and task) to corroborate that winning tickets exist and achieve near full-model performance under the chosen variance criterion.
Table 2

Starting from the concrete mask-discovery method (treat that as given), measure parameter overlap between discovered sub-networks for different task-language pairs using the Jaccard similarity $\frac{|m_i \cap m_j|}{|m_i \cup m_j|}$ computed on the binary masks $m$ obtained at a fixed sparsity (50% sparsity is used for the main analyses); note that for independent 50% masks the expected Jaccard similarity is 33%.

Compute layerwise Jaccard similarities across mBERT's 12 transformer layers for different language pairs and tasks at 50% sparsity and visualize the results to inspect absolute overlap patterns across layers and tasks.
Fig. 3

Report the observed per-task ordering of overlap magnitude at 50% sparsity: NER exhibits the largest pairwise overlap across languages, XNLI exhibits intermediate overlap, and MLM shows the smallest overlap across languages; these relative magnitudes are inferred from the layerwise Jaccard plots and accompanying text.
Fig. 3

Describe the observed layerwise patterns: for NER and XNLI, pairwise overlap between language sub-networks generally increases in higher layers; for MLM, overlap increases up to the middle layers and then decreases in the upper layers, suggesting that upper MLM layers may become more language-specialized (consistent with the intuition that MLM must predict language-specific tokens).
Fig. 3

Establish an upper bound of expected overlap by measuring same-language mask overlap across different random seeds: report that same-language masks discovered with different random seeds yield average overlaps of 98.66 for NER, 92.23 for XNLI, and 92.23 for MLM, indicating that cross-language overlaps are meaningfully lower than identical-language variability and therefore the cross-language overlap is non-trivial but not as large as intra-language reproducibility.

Starting from the pruning method and the existence of winning tickets (treat conclusions 2 and 3 as known), perform the transfer experiment that uses a source-language mask $m_s$ transferred to a target language $t$ by re-initializing unpruned parameters to $\theta_0$ and re-training on $t$; denote transferred performance as $a(s,t)$ and native target performance as $a(t,t)$ and identify successful transfers when $a(s,t)$ is within one standard deviation of $a(t,t)$.

Report the transfer results for the NER task at 50% sparsity: using the grid of transferred source-target pairs and comparing to a random 50% mask baseline, most target languages maintain roughly 98% of their native sub-network performance when trained from a source-language mask rather than from a random mask, indicating strong transferability of NER-derived masks across languages.
Fig. 4b

Report the transfer results for XNLI at 50% sparsity: many source-language masks transfer so well that English and French masks are winning tickets for other languages (i.e., the transferred performance $a(s,t)$ for English and French sources is within one standard deviation of the native $a(t,t)$ for many target languages); the Spanish, Russian, and German sub-networks also transfer well to most languages, and in some cases transferred sub-networks exceed the source performance.
Fig. 4c

Document specific notable outcomes: Arabic's winning ticket outperforms the full mBERT model by approximately $1.5$ percentage points on Swahili and Urdu for XNLI (an observed empirical improvement), and explain that Urdu and Swahili have relatively little pre-training data which may influence transfer behavior.
Fig. 4c

Report MLM transfer behavior at 50% sparsity: MLM-derived winning tickets do not become winning tickets for other languages when transferred (i.e., transferred sub-networks do not match native MLM perplexity), but perplexity increases upon transfer are relatively limited (within approximately $0.2$--$0.5$ perplexity points) compared to a random 50% sub-network, indicating MLM masks still contain shared multilingual components though they are more language-specific than XNLI or NER masks.
Fig. 4a

Note the random and additional baselines: transferring LTH-discovered sub-networks outperforms random 50% masks, and further randomization baselines (e.g., pruning discovered sub-networks at lower sparsities down to 50%) still yield higher performance than purely random masks but are outperformed by the LTH-transferred masks, supporting that discovered masks contain meaningful shared parameters.

Starting from the pruning and transfer framework (treat conclusion 2 as known), measure cross-lingual transferability of sub-networks at multiple sparsity levels (specifically compare 50% and 80% sparsity) by computing, for each source language and task, the average relative transfer performance drop across all target languages.

Define the average relative transfer performance drop used for comparison: for a fixed source language $s$ and language set $L$, compute $\frac{1}{|L|-1} \sum_{t \in L \setminus s} \frac{a(s,t)-a(t,t)}{a(t,t)}$ where $a(s,t)$ is transferred performance and $a(t,t)$ is native target performance; this is the metric plotted in the comparison.
Fig. 6

Report empirical comparison: sub-networks at 80% sparsity show substantially larger average relative performance drops when transferred across languages than sub-networks at 50% sparsity for the NER and XNLI tasks, as visualized in the bar plot comparing the two sparsity levels.
Fig. 6

Interpret the result: increasing sparsity degrades cross-lingual transferability, which the authors interpret as indicating that parameters facilitating cross-lingual transfer (i.e., language-neutral components) are preferentially removed as pruning becomes more aggressive, leaving behind parameters that are predominantly language- and task-specific and required to fit the discovering language-task pair.

Starting from the pruning and transfer methodology (treat conclusion 2 as given), repeat the cross-lingual transfer experiments on a different multilingual architecture, mT5, to test generality: mT5 is a multilingual text-to-text transformer with 12 layers and 580 million parameters pre-trained on mC4 covering 101 languages.

Formulate XNLI for mT5 in a text-to-text format by generating label text from the concatenation of premise and hypothesis (consistent with mT5 task formatting) and prune mT5 to 50% sparsity following the same iterative pruning procedure to obtain masks and sub-networks for each source language.
Xue et al. (2021)

Report transfer performance results on mT5 for XNLI at 50% sparsity: the transfer performance drops are relatively small for most source-target pairs, and similar languages (English, Spanish, French, German) transfer well to most other languages, paralleling the observations made for mBERT.
Fig. 5

Conclude that similar parameter-level language-neutral components are present in mT5 as in mBERT, evidenced by relatively modest transfer degradation and good performance of similar-language masks when transferred, indicating the phenomenon generalizes across different MultiLM architectures.

Starting from the discovered task-language sub-networks and their layerwise masks (treat conclusion 2 as known), evaluate the usefulness of these sub-networks as feature extractors in a zero-shot parallel sentence retrieval setting: encode sentences using a sub-network and use the average of token embeddings as the sentence representation for retrieval.

Describe the retrieval setup and scoring: use the English-to-French translation test set from WMT14 (3003 sentence pairs), apply the LASER parallel retrieval implementation with a margin-based scoring function $s(x,y) = \frac{\cos(x,y)}{\sum_{z \in \mathcal{N}_k(x)} \frac{\cos(x,z)}{2^k} + \sum_{z \in \mathcal{N}_k(y)} \frac{\cos(y,z)}{2^k}}$ where $x$ and $y$ are sentence representations and $\mathcal{N}_k(\cdot)$ denotes $k$-nearest neighbors, and use $\text{margin}(a,b)=a/b$ as the margin; this measures neighbor-based similarity for retrieval.
Artetxe and Schwenk (2019)

Report the empirical retrieval results by task-derived sub-network and layer: XNLI-winning tickets produce contextual features that achieve higher parallel-retrieval accuracy than MLM- or NER-derived sub-networks, and for some layers XNLI-derived sub-networks match the full mBERT model's retrieval accuracy; retrieval accuracy and representation similarity increase in the middle layers.
Fig. 7

Interpret these results: since XNLI and parallel sentence retrieval both require richer sentence-level semantic understanding, the XNLI-discovered sub-networks capture transferable semantic features in middle layers that are useful for zero-shot sentence-level semantics, implying task-conditioned sub-networks can encode transferable semantic information.

Starting from the observed parameter-overlap patterns across languages and layers (treat conclusion 4 as known), from the empirical cross-lingual transfer successes of transferred sub-networks (treat conclusion 5 as known), and from the observed sparsity-dependent degradation of transferability (treat conclusion 6 as known), synthesize these results to characterize the modular decomposition of MultiLM parameters.

Extract the first component (language-neutral parameters): note that substantial mask overlap at moderate sparsity (e.g., 50%), the ability of transferred sub-networks to retain high performance across languages (especially for XNLI and NER), and the middle-layer retrieval successes together indicate the existence of parameters that are shared across languages, survive moderate pruning, and facilitate cross-lingual transfer and zero-shot semantic tasks; label these as "language-neutral parameters".
Fig. 3
Fig. 7

Extract the second component (language- and task-specific parameters): observe that (a) increasing sparsity (e.g., 80%) substantially degrades transfer, (b) some transferred masks fail to match native performance and certain languages (e.g., Chinese, Urdu, Swahili) show larger drops, and (c) upper-layer MLM masks become more language-specialized; together these observations imply a complementary set of parameters that encode language- and task-specific information and are more sensitive to aggressive pruning.
Fig. 6

Conclude that MultiLMs empirically decompose into two separable parameter components: (a) a language-neutral subset that is shared across languages, robust to moderate pruning, and supports cross-lingual transfer and zero-shot semantic tasks, and (b) language- and task-specific parameters that are necessary to fully recover native target-language performance, especially as pruning becomes aggressive and capacity decreases.

Note the broader implication observed by the authors: cross-lingual transfer is enabled by a combination of these shared parameter subsets (which provide a transferable foundation) together with complementary language-specific parameters that must be present or recovered to fully match native performance in each language.

Starting from the pruning and transfer methodology (treat conclusion 2 as given), investigate whether combining multiple languages during pruning can produce a more language-neutral sub-network by jointly pruning on a balanced multi-language training corpus.

Describe the combined-language NER experiment: combine English (en), Farsi (fa), French (fr), and Chinese (zh) datasets with balanced sampling to create a single training corpus of 20,000 samples (25% from each language) and run the 50% iterative magnitude pruning procedure on this combined corpus to produce one 50%-sparse sub-network.

Evaluate the combined-language pruned sub-network by transferring it to several other target languages for NER and compare its transfer performance (F1) against sub-networks discovered from each individual language; present the results in the reported table which shows that the combined-language sub-network outperforms individually-discovered sub-networks for three out of five evaluated target languages.
Table 1

Interpret the result: joint pruning on multiple languages encourages recovery of more language-neutral parameters in the discovered sub-network (relative to single-language pruning), as evidenced by improved average transfer to some target languages, demonstrating that combining multiple languages for pruning can recover more language-neutral sub-networks.

open_questions.content: The study acknowledges and leaves open several scientifically meaningful issues: (1) Fine-grained mapping: which exact parameters (by layer, module, or tensor) encode language-neutral versus language-specific information remains unresolved; pairwise Jaccard overlap and coarse transfer outcomes do not fully predict small differences in cross-lingual performance. (2) Method generality: the analysis relies on the lottery-ticket iterative magnitude pruning protocol; whether alternative pruning or mask-discovery methods (structured pruning, learned masks, Fisher-based importance, sparse fine-tuning variants) would identify the same neutral components is unverified. (3) Scalability and coverage: experiments are limited to three tasks and eleven languages; whether the observed phenomena generalize across more tasks (e.g., QA, generation), more typologically diverse or extremely low-resource languages, and larger model scales is an open empirical question. (4) Causal role and transfer limits: the causal contribution of identified neutral parameters to downstream cross-lingual behavior versus confounded dataset or tokenizer effects is not fully established, nor is the maximal sparsity at which language-neutral components can be preserved without notable transfer loss. These limitations define concrete directions for future work to more precisely localize, validate, and exploit language-neutral parameter components in MultiLMs.
